metadata.name: Otitis externa (swimmer's ear)
metadata.emergency_level: Routine - but malignant (necrotising) otitis externa in diabetic/immunocompromised is an emergency

overview.short_description: Inflammation/infection of the external ear canal causing ear pain (especially on moving the ear), itch, discharge and a swollen, tender canal, usually treated with topical therapy.
overview.detailed_description: Acute otitis externa is common, often triggered by water exposure or local trauma (cotton buds). It is treated primarily with aural toilet and topical antibiotic/steroid drops. The critical exception is malignant (necrotising) otitis externa - an invasive infection (usually Pseudomonas) in older diabetics or the immunocompromised - which is an emergency.
overview.pathophysiology: Disruption of the protective cerumen barrier and canal skin (moisture, trauma, dermatitis) allows bacterial (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus) or fungal overgrowth, producing canal inflammation, oedema and discharge.
overview.etiology: Bacterial (Pseudomonas, Staph) most common; fungal (Aspergillus, Candida) especially after antibiotic drops; eczema/psoriasis predispose.
overview.natural_history: Usually resolves within days to a couple of weeks with topical treatment.
overview.prognosis: Excellent with treatment; recurrence common with ongoing water exposure. Malignant OE can be life-threatening if missed.

prevalence.value: Common, especially in swimmers and humid climates.

mortality.value: Negligible except for malignant otitis externa.

epidemiology.age_groups: All ages; malignant OE mainly older diabetics/immunocompromised.

risk_factors.lifestyle: Swimming/water exposure, humid climate, cotton-bud use, ear plugs/hearing aids, self-cleaning trauma.
risk_factors.diabetes: Major risk factor for malignant (necrotising) otitis externa.
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Eczema/psoriasis/seborrhoeic dermatitis of the canal; narrow canals.

chief_complaints.complaint: Ear pain, worse when touching/pulling the ear

symptoms.symptom: Ear pain worse on moving pinna/pressing tragus

symptoms.importance: May be scanty; fungal debris if mycotic

symptoms.symptom: Swollen, tender, erythematous ear canal +/- debris
symptoms.importance: Key examination finding; normal tympanic membrane if visible

symptoms.symptom: Severe unremitting pain, granulation tissue in canal, cranial nerve palsy (esp. diabetic/elderly)

negative_findings.finding: No pain on ear manipulation; pain worse with a normal-looking canal and abnormal drum
negative_findings.why_important: Points away from otitis externa and towards middle-ear disease

negative_findings.finding: No severe deep pain, granulation, facial weakness in a diabetic/immunocompromised patient
negative_findings.why_important: Absence argues against malignant otitis externa

history_questions.question: Is the pain worse when you touch or pull the ear?
history_questions.why_ask: Suggests external (canal) rather than middle-ear origin

history_questions.question: Any recent swimming, water exposure, or cotton-bud/ear-cleaning use?
Do you have diabetes or a weakened immune system, and is the pain severe/persistent?
Any facial weakness, severe deep-seated pain, or discharge not settling with drops?
History of eczema/psoriasis or recurrent ear problems?

physical_examination.expected_finding: Red, swollen canal with debris/discharge; tympanic membrane normal if visualised

physical_examination.examination: Assess canal patency and periauricular tissues/lymph nodes
physical_examination.expected_finding: May be swollen; spreading cellulitis suggests severity

laboratory_tests.indication: Treatment failure, recurrent, or suspected fungal/resistant infection

imaging.imaging_type: CT/MRI temporal bone + isotope bone scan

other_diagnostic_tests.endoscopy: Microsuction/aural toilet by ENT for debris clearance
other_diagnostic_tests.biopsy: Granulation tissue biopsy if malignant OE/neoplasm suspected
other_diagnostic_tests.culture: Swab of discharge in resistant/complicated cases

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Clinical: rapid onset of ear canal symptoms (pain, itch, fullness) WITH signs of canal inflammation (tenderness on tragus/pinna movement, canal oedema/erythema, +/- discharge), with an intact/normal tympanic membrane where visible.

differential_diagnosis.differences: Deep pain, no pain on ear manipulation, abnormal/bulging drum, preceding URTI
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is it painful to pull the ear, or is the pain deeper inside?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Marked itch, fluffy/black-spore debris, often after antibiotic drops
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Very itchy and did drops not help?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Severe unremitting pain, granulation tissue, cranial nerve palsy, diabetic/immunocompromised
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_exam: Granulation at bony-cartilaginous junction, CN palsy
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Are you diabetic with severe persistent ear pain or facial weakness?
Any object placed in the ear or ongoing skin problems?

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the pain clearly worse when you press the tragus or pull the ear?
Do you have diabetes/immunosuppression with severe persistent pain or facial weakness?

next_best_question.current_situation: Ear pain with inflamed canal on otoscopy
next_best_question.question: Is it painful to move the ear, and do you have diabetes or a weak immune system?
next_best_question.expected_answers: Simple OE vs at-risk for necrotising
next_best_question.branching_logic: Simple OE -> aural toilet + topical drops + keep dry; at-risk with severe/persistent pain, granulation, or CN palsy -> urgent ENT for necrotising OE

next_best_test.why: Confirms canal inflammation and clears debris for treatment

next_best_test.test: CT/MRI + inflammatory markers (only if malignant OE suspected)

red_flags.finding: Diabetic/immunocompromised with severe, unremitting or night-time ear pain
red_flags.immediate_action: Urgent ENT - suspect malignant otitis externa

red_flags.finding: Granulation tissue in the canal, facial or other cranial nerve palsy
Spreading periauricular cellulitis, fever, or systemic illness
Not improving with appropriate topical treatment
red_flags.immediate_action: Reassess (fungal, resistant, or alternative diagnosis); consider ENT

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Suspected malignant otitis externa; severe/spreading infection; need for microsuction not available in primary care.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Recurrent/chronic otitis externa; persistent debris needing aural toilet; suspected canal stenosis.
referral_criteria.emergency_referral: Necrotising otitis externa with cranial nerve involvement.

initial_management.supportive_care: Analgesia; keep the ear dry; aural toilet (microsuction/dry mopping) to remove debris improves topical treatment.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Non-ototoxic topical antimicrobial with or without corticosteroid; Paracetamol; NSAID; Systemic antibiotic. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: AAOHNS_AOE_2014.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Keep water out of the ear (avoid swimming) during treatment; do not use cotton buds; treat underlying skin conditions.
initial_management.follow_up: Review if not improving; consider swab, aural toilet, or ENT referral.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Topical antibiotic +/- corticosteroid ear drops/spray (e.g., aminoglycoside or quinolone with steroid) for 7-14 days; use an ear wick if the canal is very swollen. Topical antifungal if fungal. Oral antibiotics only if spreading cellulitis/systemic illness or immunocompromise. Avoid aminoglycoside drops if the drum is known to be perforated (use quinolone).

patient_education.home_advice: Swimmer's ear is inflammation of the ear canal, often after water or ear-cleaning. Ear drops usually clear it in about a week. Keep the ear dry, don't use cotton buds, and take painkillers. See a doctor urgently if you have diabetes or a weak immune system with severe or lasting pain, or if you develop facial weakness.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: أذن السبّاح التهاب في قناة الأذن، غالباً بعد الماء أو تنظيف الأذن. تشفيها القطرات عادةً خلال أسبوع. أبقِ الأذن جافة، ولا تستخدم أعواد القطن، وتناول مسكّنات الألم. راجع الطبيب فوراً إذا كنت مصاباً بالسكري أو ضعف المناعة مع ألم شديد أو مستمر، أو إذا ظهر ضعف في عضلات الوجه.
patient_education.prevention: Dry ears after swimming, avoid cotton buds, consider acidifying/drying drops for frequent swimmers, treat eczema.
patient_education.warning_signs: Severe or persistent pain (especially if diabetic), facial weakness, spreading redness/swelling, fever, or no improvement with drops.

prevention.lifestyle: Keep ears dry, avoid trauma/cotton buds; drying drops for frequent swimmers.

evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by AAOHNS_AOE_2014; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
